prompt: Who decides when an app's background sync runs, on Android and on iOS?

choices.text: The app, with a timer it sets for itself
choices.why: Neither platform offers that; the app asks.

choices.text: The server, by pushing a message when it has changes
choices.why: The lesson's mechanisms are scheduled by the system, not started by a server.

choices.text: The system
choices.why: Right. It decides when, for how long and whether at all, to protect the battery.

choices.text: The person, from a setting in the app
choices.why: The person can stop it, but cannot schedule it.

prompt: Match each mechanism to what it does to background work.

pairs.right: suspends network and defers jobs on an idle, unplugged phone
run an app's jobs less often the less it is used

pairs.left: an app refresh task on iOS
pairs.right: about thirty seconds, when the system chooses

pairs.left: swiping the app away on iOS
pairs.right: no background launches until it is opened again

right_distractors: a guaranteed run every fifteen minutes

prompt: Why does the lesson say background sync must never be the only path?

choices.text: It runs when the system allows, so the app syncs on launch and on save too
choices.why: Right. A background run only shortens the queue.

choices.text: Stores reject apps that sync in the background
choices.why: Both platforms provide the APIs this lesson quotes.

choices.text: Background code cannot open the database
choices.why: It can; lesson 16's React Native task opens it itself.

choices.text: It drains the battery faster than a foreground sync
choices.why: Battery is why the system limits it, not why it must have company.

prompt: What is the shortest period, in minutes, that WorkManager accepts for periodic work?
The planner calls enqueueUniquePeriodicWork with KEEP on every launch. What happens on the tenth launch?

choices.text: WorkManager throws, because the name is taken
choices.why: The policy says what to do with a taken name.

choices.text: A tenth job is queued beside the other nine
choices.why: That is what unique work exists to prevent.

choices.text: The period restarts from that launch
choices.why: That is REPLACE.

choices.text: Nothing new: the existing job is kept
choices.why: Right. Unique work with KEEP schedules one job, not one per launch.

prompt: What does returning Result.retry() from the worker do?

choices.text: Runs doWork again at once, in the same process
choices.why: WorkManager waits first, by the backoff it was given.

choices.text: Hands it back to WorkManager to run later, with backoff
choices.why: Right. The exponential backoff of lesson 9, done for you.

choices.text: Shows the person an error with a retry button
choices.why: A worker has no screen.

choices.text: Cancels the periodic work for good
choices.why: That would be failure, and even then the periodic request stays.

prompt: Where must the planner list the identifier org.example.planner.refresh before iOS will schedule it?

choices.text: In App Store Connect
choices.why: Scheduling is checked on the device, against the app's own files.

choices.text: In BGTaskSchedulerPermittedIdentifiers, in Info.plist
choices.why: Right. The system refuses a name it does not find there.

choices.text: In UserDefaults, written the first time the app opens on the device
choices.why: Preferences are data; the permission is in the app's declaration.

choices.text: Nowhere; any identifier works
choices.why: It has to be declared.

prompt: What does iOS do when it calls the refresh task's expirationHandler?

choices.text: Saying the sync finished successfully
choices.why: The app says that, with setTaskCompleted.

choices.text: Granting thirty more seconds
choices.why: It is the end of the time, not an extension.

choices.text: Asking the app to schedule the next refresh
choices.why: The app schedules the next one first, without being asked.

choices.text: Saying the time is up
choices.why: Right. The handler cancels the sync, which stops with its progress saved.

prompt: A planner's refresh task works for a day, then never runs again. Its handler syncs and calls setTaskCompleted. What is the most likely mistake in the lesson's terms?

choices.text: It never submits the next request
choices.why: Right. A refresh request is used once; the handler must ask for the next.

choices.text: The identifier is missing from Info.plist
choices.why: Then it would never have run at all.

choices.text: setTaskCompleted is called too early, so iOS blocks the app
choices.why: Finishing early is allowed; overrunning is what costs chances.

choices.text: The sync uses URLSession instead of a background session
choices.why: A short sync inside a refresh can use an ordinary session.

prompt: What is true of a background URLSession upload, according to the lesson? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: it must come from a file
choices.why: The app may not be alive to hand over bytes.

choices.text: it carries on after the system terminates the app
choices.why: The system runs the transfer and wakes the app afterwards.

choices.text: it survives the person swiping the app away
choices.why: Swiping away cancels background transfers too.

choices.text: it is limited to thirty seconds
choices.why: That is the refresh task, not a background transfer.

prompt: Why must the planner's TaskManager.defineTask call sit at the top level of a module?

choices.text: Expo compiles top-level code into Kotlin and Swift
choices.why: The task stays JavaScript; nothing is compiled into another language.

choices.text: Components are not allowed to import expo-task-manager
choices.why: Imports are not the issue; when the code runs is.

choices.text: The system starts the app for it with no screen and nothing mounted
choices.why: Right. A task defined in a component would not exist yet.

choices.text: Top-level code runs on a faster thread
choices.why: Placement does not change the thread.

prompt: With the app open, a background sync and a sync started by a screen run at once. What does the lesson say keeps them from sending the outbox twice?

choices.text: The outbox rows record what is in flight, and keys absorb a duplicate
choices.why: Right. State on disk is shared by every launch; lesson 10's keys catch the rest.

choices.text: A boolean in memory set by whichever starts first
choices.why: A closed app's task is a fresh launch that never saw the flag.

choices.text: expo-background-task waits until the app is closed
choices.why: Nothing in the lesson says it waits.

choices.text: React Native runs one JavaScript function at a time, so they cannot overlap
choices.why: Both are async and interleave at every await.

prompt: In bg.ts, what makes the point between two steps a safe place to stop?

choices.text: Each run asks the system how long it has
choices.why: No platform tells it; that is the premise.

choices.text: Each step runs in a separate process
choices.why: One process runs all its steps.

choices.text: A checkpoint is written after each step
choices.why: Right. The outbox row is marked sent, or the cursor moves on.

choices.text: The program catches SIGKILL and saves before exiting
choices.why: SIGKILL cannot be caught; nothing is saved at the end.

prompt: In the lesson's runs, how many operations were still waiting to be sent when the first run, with four steps, stopped?
The process was killed after k6 reached the server and before the outbox marked it. Without idempotency keys, what would the next run have done for an operation that adds a session?

choices.text: Skipped it, because the server had answered
choices.why: The device never saw the answer; the kill came first.

choices.text: Added it a second time
choices.why: Right. The work was done and the record of it was not.

choices.text: Lost it, because the outbox row was deleted
choices.why: The row was still there, unsent, which is why it was sent again.

choices.text: Asked the person whether to send it
choices.why: A background run has nobody to ask.

prompt: Put the iOS refresh handler of the lesson in order.
items: start the sync as a Task
set the expirationHandler to cancel it
wait for the sync to end

prompt: A background sync is safe to stop when it works in small steps and writes a ___ after each one.
A planner's sync downloads every page first and writes them all, with the cursor, at the end. It runs in a thirty-second refresh task. What happens on a phone with a slow network?

choices.text: iOS extends the task until the download finishes
choices.why: The time is the system's; it does not wait.

choices.text: The pages are saved anyway when the task expires
choices.why: Nothing is written until the end, and the end never comes.

choices.text: It finishes on the next run, since the cursor moved
choices.why: The cursor is written at the end, so it never moved.

choices.text: Every run is stopped before the end, and none gets further than the last
choices.why: Right. Being stopped costs the whole run, every time.
